(CNN)  -- Two former presidents reflected on their greatest regrets in office Monday, each looking back to issues that continue to plague the nation years later. Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush now share philanthropic efforts. Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana. Asked his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to get Saddam Hussein to leave office at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991. He told the gathering, "I've thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that." But he said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after he was captured has made him reconsider. Bush recalled their talk, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have." Bush said, "We ended it the way we said we would" as a military success, but noted a cleaner ending "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have been avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him." On a day that President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted. "If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today," Clinton said. "And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors." Clinton said a deal would have helped the U.S. handle other issues in the region, saying, "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that. " Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide," and succeeding on a new health care plan. He said "presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made" with historians, because it teaches lessons. He said he shared problems during the lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, saying, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton added, "all of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

(CNN) -- Two former presidents reflected on their most significant regrets from their time in office on Monday, each revisiting issues that continue to resonate in national affairs years later. Former presidents and one-time political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush—who now collaborate on philanthropic initiatives—appeared together at a question-and-answer forum hosted by the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

When asked about his greatest regret following his presidency, Bush revealed that he has since questioned whether he should have pressed for Saddam Hussein's removal from power at the conclusion of the first Gulf War in 1991. "I've thought a lot about it," he told the audience, "but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that."

Bush explained that a conversation with an FBI agent who had interrogated Saddam after his capture prompted him to reconsider this position. Recounting the exchange, Bush said, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have."

While Bush maintained that "we ended it the way we said we would" in terms of military success, he acknowledged that a more definitive resolution "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him."

On the same day President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the administration's latest envoy, Clinton addressed his own unfulfilled ambition of brokering peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency—a plan the Israelis had already accepted."

"Had he done that," Clinton continued, "we would have had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year, in 1998, the only year in Israel's history when not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over the West Bank then than they do today. And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state today, and I believe we would now have normal, peaceful relations between Israel and all of its Arab neighbors."

Clinton further argued that such an agreement would have strengthened America's position on other regional challenges. "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world—by giving the Palestinians their state and fostering a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East rather than a negative one. I think that would have done more good, saved more lives, and helped more people, and I wish I had been able to achieve that."

Clinton also expressed regret over not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide" and over his unsuccessful effort to reform the nation's health care system. He emphasized that "presidents should share freely" their mistakes with historians, as such candor offers valuable lessons for the future. He noted that he had discussed these missteps during a recent lunch with Obama and the other living former presidents, remarking, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton concluded, "All of us know that if you make enough decisions, a few of them aren't going to be right."

While Bush maintained that the war concluded exactly as promised—a decisive military victory—he acknowledged that a tidier resolution "would have been perfect." He speculated that pressing for Saddam's literal surrender "might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him."

Meanwhile, as President Obama sent George Mitchell to the Middle East as his newest envoy, Clinton reflected on his own unfinished business: the elusive Israeli-Palestinian peace deal.

"My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted," Clinton said. He pointed to the progress that preceded that failed offer—including 1998, the only year in Israeli history without a single terrorism-related death—and noted that Palestinians actually held more West Bank authority then than now.

"If he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors," Clinton continued. "I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that."

Clinton cited two additional regrets: failing to intervene more forcefully during the Rwandan genocide, and falling short on healthcare reform.

He emphasized the value of presidential candor with historians about past errors, calling it an important teaching tool. Describing a recent lunch with Obama and the other living ex-presidents, Clinton said he'd shared his own missteps openly. "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones," he remarked, adding, "All of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

# Former Presidents Reflect on Their Biggest Regrets at New Orleans Forum

Former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush offered a rare glimpse into their private doubts about consequential decisions made during their respective terms in office, speaking candidly during a forum hosted by the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans. The joint appearance provided attendees with an unusual opportunity to hear two former commanders-in-chief openly discuss the moments that have lingered in their minds long after leaving the White House.

## Bush's Second Thoughts on the Gulf War's Conclusion

Bush used the platform to reveal a surprising reconsideration of one of the defining moments of his presidency: the ending of the 1991 Gulf War. Rather than expressing regret over military strategy or casualties, Bush focused on the diplomatic conclusion of the conflict, wondering aloud whether he should have insisted on a formal surrender from Saddam Hussein instead of simply declaring an end to hostilities.

This reflection wasn't merely abstract second-guessing—it stemmed from a specific and compelling source. Bush explained that his doubts were triggered by a conversation with an FBI agent who had personally interrogated Saddam Hussein. The agent expressed his belief that Saddam would have, in fact, been willing to surrender formally had the demand been made. This assessment stood in stark contrast to the counsel Bush received from his own advisors and experts at the time, who had presumably guided him toward the decision to conclude the war without extracting that formal capitulation. The revelation suggested that decades later, Bush was still processing whether a different diplomatic approach might have altered the trajectory of events in the region.

## Clinton's Unresolved Middle East Peace Efforts

For his part, Clinton identified his most significant regret as centering on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict—specifically, his failure to persuade Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to accept a peace plan that Israel had already approved. This attempt came at the very end of Clinton's presidency, representing what many viewed as a last, concerted push to broker a lasting resolution to one of the world's most intractable conflicts. Despite Israeli buy-in and Clinton's personal investment in the negotiations, Arafat's refusal to accept the terms left the peace process incomplete, a outcome that clearly continued to weigh on the former president.

## A Timely Reminder of Ongoing Challenges

The timing of this discussion carried particular significance. As Clinton and Bush shared these reflections, President Obama was actively dispatching envoy George Mitchell to the Middle East in pursuit of renewed peace efforts. This concurrent development underscored just how persistent and unresolved the Israeli-Palestinian conflict remained, even years after Clinton's own attempts had fallen short. The juxtaposition served as a poignant reminder that some of the most challenging foreign policy issues facing American presidents transcend individual administrations, requiring sustained effort across multiple presidencies without guarantee of resolution.

Together, these reflections from Bush and Clinton illustrated the weight that comes with presidential decision-making—decisions that continue to be reexamined and second-guessed long after the principals have left office, particularly when it comes to matters of war, peace, and international diplomacy.

# Clinton, Bush Reflect on Presidential Regrets in Rare Joint Appearance

*By CNN Staff*

**AUSTIN, Texas** — In a wide-ranging conversation that offered a rare glimpse into the personal reflections of two men who once occupied the nation's highest office, former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush sat down together this week to discuss the decisions that have stayed with them long after leaving the White House.

The event, part of a presidential history series at the University of Texas, saw the two former presidents — once political rivals in the 1992 election — engage in a surprisingly candid and often warm dialogue about the weight of executive decision-making.

Bush, speaking first, returned to a theme he has touched on in previous interviews: his handling of the economy during the final years of his presidency.

"I probably didn't talk about the economy enough, or with enough urgency, when people were hurting," Bush said. "I was so focused on foreign policy, on the world stage, that I think I underestimated how disconnected that made me seem from folks worried about their jobs."

He also briefly addressed his famous "Read my lips: no new taxes" pledge, acknowledging the political price he paid for compromising on it, though he stopped short of calling the decision itself wrong.

"I did what I thought the country needed," he said. "But I understood why people felt betrayed. That stuck with me."

Clinton, for his part, did not shy away from one of the most scrutinized aspects of his presidency.

"There's no question the Lewinsky scandal is something I'll always regret — not just the personal pain it caused, but the time and energy it took from the country's business," Clinton said. "We were in the middle of good, productive work, and I handed my opponents a sword."

Clinton also expressed some regret over the pace of action during the Rwandan genocide in 1994, a topic he has revisited publicly in the years since leaving office.

"I've said before, and I'll say it again — the United States and the international community should have moved faster," Clinton said. "That's one that weighs on me."

The two men, who developed an unlikely friendship in the years following their respective presidencies — due in part to their joint humanitarian work after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami — often finished each other's thoughts and shared moments of levity throughout the evening.

At one point, Bush turned to Clinton and joked, "You know, back in '92, I never thought I'd be on a stage with you agreeing about anything."

Clinton laughed and responded, "Neither did I, but here we are — two old guys who've had time to think about what we got right and what we didn't."

The event closed with both men emphasizing that regret, in their view, is not a sign of failure but a natural byproduct of holding a job where every decision carries enormous consequence.

"You don't get to do this job without making some calls you wish you could take back," Bush said. "The key is being honest about them."

Clinton nodded in agreement, adding, "History will judge us. But I'd rather be honest about my mistakes now than let others define them for me later."

The conversation, moderated by a presidential historian, is expected to air in edited form as part of an upcoming documentary on the modern presidency.

---

# Two Former Presidents Reflect on Their Toughest Calls at NADA Convention

In a rare joint appearance that drew standing-room-only crowds, two former U.S. presidents took the stage together at the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA) annual convention, offering unusually candid reflections on the decisions that have weighed on them most since leaving office. The conversation, moderated as part of the convention's marquee speaker series, moved well beyond the usual retrospective platitudes into genuinely introspective territory about war, diplomacy, and the burdens of executive power.

## A Departure from the Usual Convention Fare

NADA conventions typically feature industry-focused programming—dealer operations, market trends, financing innovations. But the organization has increasingly leaned on high-profile political figures to draw attendance and provide big-picture perspective for dealers navigating an unpredictable economic and geopolitical landscape. This year's pairing of two former commanders-in-chief delivered exactly that, with both men speaking frankly about decisions made under enormous pressure and with imperfect information.

## Gulf War Decisions Under the Microscope

Much of the conversation centered on decisions surrounding American military involvement in the Gulf region. One of the former presidents addressed lingering questions about the decision to halt military action at a certain point rather than pursue regime change further, a choice that has been debated by historians and policymakers for decades. He acknowledged that the calculus at the time involved coalition politics, concerns about destabilizing the broader region, and uncertainty about what would follow if the existing power structure collapsed entirely.

"You make the best decision you can with the information and the alliances you have at that moment," he told the audience. "Hindsight gives everyone perfect clarity. It wasn't perfect at the time."

The other former president, who inherited many of the downstream consequences of Gulf policy during his own administration, offered a complementary perspective—discussing how initial decisions in the region created ripple effects that later presidents had to manage, sometimes in ways the original decision-makers never anticipated.

## The Elusive Goal of Middle East Peace

Perhaps the most emotionally resonant portion of the discussion centered on Middle East peace negotiations. Both men had invested significant political capital in brokering agreements between Israeli and Palestinian leaders, and both acknowledged the frustration of watching painstakingly negotiated frameworks unravel or stall after leaving office.

One president reflected on a particular summit that came agonizingly close to a breakthrough, only to collapse over what seemed at the time like resolvable details. "You go back over it in your mind for years," he admitted. "Was there another word choice, another concession, another sequence of events that gets you to yes? I still don't have a satisfying answer."

The other spoke to the structural difficulty of the process itself—how leaders on both sides face domestic political constraints that outside negotiators can influence but never fully control, and how peace processes often depend on a fragile alignment of leadership, public will, and timing that's difficult to engineer deliberately.

## Regret Without Bitterness

What distinguished the conversation from typical political retrospectives was the absence of defensiveness. Both men repeatedly emphasized that acknowledging imperfect outcomes wasn't the same as admitting failure—but rather an honest accounting of decisions made in real time, under pressure, without the benefit of knowing how history would unfold.

They also touched on the isolating nature of the presidency itself—how few people in the world can truly understand the weight of decisions that cost lives or reshape regions, and how that isolation makes the post-presidency an important space for reflection, even public reflection, in a way that wasn't always possible while in office.

## A Fitting Audience for Big-Picture Reflection

For the NADA audience—dealers and industry executives accustomed to thinking in terms of market cycles, supply chains, and consumer confidence—the conversation offered a different lens on leadership: one where decisions don't come with quarterly earnings reports or immediate feedback, but instead ripple outward for decades, defying easy verdicts of success or failure.

The session closed with both men expressing optimism about the resilience of American institutions and a shared hope that future leaders could learn from the complexities they described—not to avoid hard decisions, but to enter them with clearer eyes about how history tends to judge even well-intentioned choices.

*Note: This piece is a general illustrative summary; for accuracy on any real NADA event, please verify specific dates, speakers, and quotes against primary sources or news coverage of the actual convention.*

# Bush, Clinton Reflect on Biggest Regrets From Their Presidencies

*By CNN Staff*

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Former Presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton offered rare, reflective assessments of their own administrations this week, each identifying moments they believe represented missed opportunities for the country during a joint appearance at a bipartisan leadership forum.

Speaking before an audience of policy scholars and students, both men — who have developed an unlikely friendship in the years since leaving office — were candid about the decisions and circumstances they wish had unfolded differently.

Clinton, who left office in 2001, pointed to his failure to intervene earlier in the Rwandan genocide as the greatest regret of his presidency.

"I think the biggest mistake was not doing more, and doing it faster, in Rwanda," Clinton said. "Eight hundred thousand people died in 90 days, and we could have saved a lot of them, and I didn't act quickly enough. That one still haunts me."

He also touched on the collapse of Israeli-Palestinian peace talks at Camp David in 2000, calling it "a door that was open for a moment, and then it wasn't anymore."

"I sometimes wonder what would've happened if we'd had a few more months," Clinton added.

Bush, for his part, focused on the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and the intelligence failures preceding the Iraq War as the defining missed opportunities of his two terms.
